newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian government wins confidence vote over budget.
newsitem.headline: Italian government wins confidence vote over budget.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi easily won a confidence vote in the lower house of parliament on Tuesday, called to sweep aside opposition amendments to the final section of the 1997 austerity budget.

Prodi won the do-or-die vote thanks to the backing of Communist Refoundation, but faces a tougher battle convincing his hard-left ally to accept a fresh dose of budgetary rigour that the government is preparing.

Prodi met Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti early on Tuesday to persuade him of the need for more deficit-cutting measures in an effort to prepare Italy for the launch of European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Bertinotti promised to support Tuesday's confidence motion, which was carried by 308 votes to 257, with one abstention, but he repeated his concerns about another round of belt-tightening.
"We consider a mini-budget to be unnecessary, and if it was up to us we would not do it," Bertinotti said.
"But the government thinks it is necessary so we are open to talks," he told reporters, adding that Refoundation could not accept any further cut in social spending or additional taxes.

Italy has adopted a series of increasingly tough budgets over the past five years in a bid to repair the damage done by free-spending administrations at the end of the 1980s and become a founder member of the single European currency.
The latest package of measures, which was mostly approved by parliament last December, was designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($37.5 billion) off the public sector deficit in 1997.

However the final segment, which accounts for 4.3 trillion lire of savings, was only introduced as a cabinet decree. Its passage onto the statute books was threatened by a wave of amendments, forcing the government to hold the confidence vote.
Prodi, who took office last May, had hoped that the 1997 budget would be enough to allow Italy a place at the birth of EMU, but his plans were wrecked by an unexpected surge in 1996 state spending.
To mop up the overshoot, he announced last week that his centre-left cabinet was working on a new mini-budget, which would focus on structural changes.
Analysts expect it to include up to 15 trillion lire of deficit cuts and many have urged Prodi to prune welfare spending -- especially the generous state pensions system.
News of yet more budget medicine received a frosty reception from left wingers and the largest trades' union, the Cgil.
"A mini-budget is useless and unwelcome," Cgil leader Sergio Cofferati told La Stampa newspaper on Tuesday.

But Prodi got backing for his crusade to tame the deficit from European Union Commissioner, Mario Monti, who said on Tuesday that Italy needed to be in the vanguard of EMU to boost employment and production prospects.

"Today one can say that Italy probably will take part in the single currency," Monti told a parliamentary committee in Rome. Only a few months ago...it seemed certain that it would be excluded. Italy has taken a major step forward," he added.
